name: Olafur Eliasson
bio: Olafur Eliasson (born 1967) grew up between Denmark and Iceland and studied at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts. He runs a large studio in Berlin of craftspeople, architects, technicians and researchers. His work uses light, water, fog, mirrors, colour and temperature to make people aware of how they perceive. The weather project (2003) filled Tate Modern's Turbine Hall with a huge artificial sun in a haze, and visitors lay on the floor to watch themselves in the mirrored ceiling. He has made artificial waterfalls in New York (2008), a ring-shaped rainbow walkway on the roof of ARoS in Aarhus (Your rainbow panorama, 2011), blocks of Greenland ice left to melt in city squares (Ice Watch, from 2014), and the solar-powered lamp Little Sun (2012). He has increasingly turned his studio towards climate and social questions.
studyNotes: Show the mechanism. He often leaves the machinery (lamps, pumps, scaffolding) visible, so you see both the effect and how it is made.
Viewers as the subject. Mirrors, coloured light and fog turn the audience into part of the picture; the work is about seeing yourself seeing.
Phenomena over objects. Weather, colour and reflection are the material; he builds conditions rather than things.
A studio as a lab. Look at the range of research, models and collaborations; the large works rest on years of small experiments with light and geometry.
